1. Written sources and the purpose of this chapter

Four core courses supply complementary foundations: Oxford Prelims Probability by James Martin; Cambridge Introduction to Probability by Mateja Jamnik and Thomas Sauerwald; Berkeley CS 70 by Rao and Walrand; and MIT 18.05 written notes by Jeremy Orloff and Jonathan Bloom. Chris Piech's Stanford CS 109 Poisson slides supply an additional reviewed application perspective. Exact page ranges, candidate decisions and corrected source statements are in the source audit. These materials were actually read; an unread course title is not a source contribution.

Earlier chapters introduced random variables and moments. Here the objective is to derive, recognize and manipulate the named discrete laws under explicit experimental contracts. A formula is useful only after its support, parameter convention, stopping rule and independence conditions are identified. The theory, worked bank and final notes connect these contracts to numerical and conceptual examination questions.

2. Begin with the experiment, not the distribution name

A Bernoulli trial is a binary observation with success probability p and failure probability q=1-p. An independent identically distributed sequence means that every finite collection of specified outcomes has probability equal to the product of its individual probabilities. Pairwise independence alone is weaker and does not establish a binomial count law.

Three questions about the same sequence define different random variables. The number of successes among a fixed number n of trials is a binomial count. The number of trials through the first success is a positive geometric waiting time. The number of trials through the r th success is a negative-binomial waiting time. The last two have random horizons; their final trials are forced successes. That final constraint changes the combinatorial coefficient.

Sampling a fixed-size subset without replacement uses a hypergeometric count because successive draws deplete a finite population. A Poisson law is an unbounded count model with a dimensionless expected count parameter. The average count alone never establishes that model.

Before calculating, write a sentence defining the random variable, list its possible values, identify every random input and specify which inputs are independent. A count of eligible successes is not a count of attempted trials. A deterministic horizon cannot be replaced by its average when the horizon is random.

3. Bernoulli laws and what two moments can establish

For B∈{0,1} with P(B=1)=p, the complete law is

P(B=0)=q,P(B=1)=p,0≤p≤1.

Because every positive integer power equals the indicator itself, E[Bm]=p for m≥1. Thus

E[B]=p,Var(B)=pq,GB(z)=q+pz.

The variance is at most 1/4, attained at p=1/2. A given variance below that maximum usually admits two success probabilities related by reflection. Its mean resolves that ambiguity.

The converse needs a support condition. If a real variable is known to lie in [0,1] and satisfies E[X]=E[X2], then E[X(1-X)]=0. The nonnegative integrand must vanish almost surely, so X is supported on the endpoints and is Bernoulli. Without the interval restriction, an equality of two moments need not force a binary law.

At p=0 or p=1 the law is constant. Its variance is zero and Pearson correlation with another variable is undefined. These endpoints are legitimate count laws; geometric success waiting at p=0 requires a different extended-valued interpretation.

4. Deriving the binomial law by grouping sequences

Let B1,…,Bn be mutually independent Bernoulli variables with common probability p, and set Sn=∑i=1nBi. A specified sequence with k successes has probability pkqn-k. There are (nk) positions for those successes. Therefore

P(Sn=k)=(nk)pkqn-k,k=0,…,n.

Disjoint sequences justify addition; independence justifies multiplication within each sequence; identical probabilities justify assigning every sequence in the group the same weight. Omitting any one of these steps can invalidate the binomial formula.

Normalization follows from the binomial theorem: the sum of the masses is (p+q)n=1. Define the endpoint laws directly to avoid interpreting an ambiguous 00 term: if p=0, all mass is at zero; if p=1, all mass is at n. At n=0 the empty count is also zero.

For four independent objects that each qualify with probability 1/2 and then independently succeed with probability 1/2, a final success has probability 1/4. The resulting count is binomial with four trials and probability 1/4, not a fair binomial with an average of two trials.

Count propagation with probabilities 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5

This is an exact probability-law mechanism with declared sample inputs, not a random demonstration or a universal proof. Finite displays retain or label unresolved tail mass.

5. Factorial moments and generating functions

The probability generating function, defined by GX(z)=E[zX], encodes a nonnegative integer law. Its coefficients recover the masses, so equal PGFs near zero imply equal laws. Independent sums multiply PGFs; a scaled copy uses substitution instead.

For the binomial law,

GSn(z)=(q+pz)n.

Differentiate j times and evaluate at one:

E[(Sn)j]=(n)jpj,

where (x)j=x(x-1)…(x-j+1) and (x)0=1. There is also a counting proof: expand the factorial count as a sum over ordered distinct success positions. Each ordered j -tuple contributes probability pj, and there are (n)j such tuples. For j>n the factorial moment is zero.

In particular,

E[Sn]=np,E[Sn(Sn-1)]=n(n-1)p2,
Var(Sn)=n(n-1)p2+np-n2p2=npq.

The second derivative is a factorial moment, not a raw second moment. Restore the missing first moment using X2=X(X-1)+X. More generally a fixed number of independent copies and a deterministic multiple are different operations: GX1+…+Xm(z)=GX(z)m, while GmX(z)=GX(zm).

6. Adjacent ratios, modes and recovering parameters

For an interior binomial law with 0<p<1,

P(Sn=k+1)P(Sn=k)=n-kk+1pq.

The ratio is above one precisely when k+1<(n+1)p. If (n+1)p is not an integer, the unique mode is its floor. If it equals an integer m with 1≤m≤n, the adjacent modes are m-1 and m. Endpoint laws have their single deterministic modes. A mean is not automatically a mode, and a tied ratio must not be discarded.

Suppose a claimed binomial law has mean μ>0 and variance v. Then v=μ(1-p), so p=1-v/μ and n=μ/p when p>0. These equations are necessary; they must yield an admissible probability and an integer trial count. If v=μ>0, no finite nondegenerate binomial law satisfies them. If v=0, a binomial law is deterministic and its positive mean must equal an integer horizon.

An adjacent probability ratio can identify p only when n and the two support indices are known. A zero denominator or an endpoint law requires direct analysis rather than division.

7. Complements, parity, tails and conditional counts

The failure count n-Sn is binomial with success probability q. Thus a lower tail can be reflected into an upper tail without changing the number of trials. For a fair law and odd n, symmetry gives P(Sn≤(n-1)/2)=1/2. For even n the central atom must be handled separately.

Parity is encoded by the PGF at minus one:

E[(-1)Sn]=(q-p)n.

Since even outcomes contribute one and odd outcomes contribute minus one,

P(Sn is even)=1+(1-2p)n2.

Conditioning changes the law. Given Sn=k with positive probability and 0<p<1, every success-position subset of size k has the same conditional probability 1/(nk). The number of successes among the first m trials is then hypergeometric:

P(Sm=j∣Sn=k)=(mj)(n-mk-j)(nk).

The successes inside the conditioned horizon are dependent. A product of the original marginal probabilities is not a conditional joint probability.

For integer-valued X, translate a noninteger threshold before summing: P(X<t)=P(X≤⌈t⌉-1) and P(X≤t)=P(X≤⌊t⌋). The distinction is especially important at an integer endpoint.

8. Thinning, classification and dependence after splitting

Let N∼Bin(n,p). Independently retain each success with probability a. Define K as the retained count. Each original trial becomes retained with probability pa, so K∼Bin(n,pa). Conditioning on N gives a second proof through PGF composition:

GK(z)=GN(1-a+az)=(1-pa+paz)n.

Classify each trial into retained success, rejected success and original failure, with probabilities pa,p(1-a),q. Their joint count law is multinomial. Retained and rejected counts have covariance -np2a(1-a) because one fixed trial cannot contribute to both categories. They are generally not independent, despite independent marking of each object.

This contrasts with Poisson splitting, where a random unbounded total produces independent classified counts. The difference is in the total-count law, not in whether the marks were chosen independently.

9. Unequal trials and the Poisson-binomial distribution

Independent indicators with probabilities p1,…,pn have count PGF

GS(z)=∏i=1n(1-pi+piz).

Their mean is ∑ipi and their variance is ∑ipi(1-pi). A common average probability generally does not give the same law. In fact, if p¯ is the average,

np¯(1-p¯)-Var(S)=∑i(pi-p¯)2.

The heterogeneous count has smaller variance than the common-probability independent count with the same mean. A shared latent probability creates the opposite kind of effect and must not be confused with fixed unequal probabilities.

To compute all masses, start with a0=1. Incorporating a new probability p uses bk=(1-p)ak+pak-1, with out-of-range entries zero. These are two mutually exclusive ways to reach the new success count. Update a separate buffer, or update indices in descending order; an ascending in-place update would reuse values from the current trial and overcount.

10. Geometric support, survival and two conventions

Let T be the number of iid Bernoulli trials through the first success, with 0<p≤1. For 0<p<1,

P(T=t)=qt-1p,t=1,2,….

The first t-1 trials must fail and the final trial must succeed. There is no binomial coefficient because only one terminal pattern is allowed. Let F=T-1 be the failures before success; then P(F=f)=qfp for f≥0.

For integers m≥0, P(T>m)=qm. Hence for real x≥1,

P(T≤x)=1-q⌊x⌋.

For x<1 the CDF is zero. Positive and zero-based means differ by one, while their variances agree:

E[T]=1/p,E[F]=q/p,Var(T)=Var(F)=q/p2.

One derivation differentiates ∑j≥0zj=(1-z)-1 inside its convergence radius. Another uses the tail-sum identity E[T]=∑m≥0P(T>m). A first-step second-moment recursion gives E[T2]=p+qE[(1+T')2], where T' is an independent fresh wait with the same law. Substituting the mean yields E[T2]=(2-p)/p2.

At p=1, T=1 and F=0. At p=0, success never occurs; no probability-one finite waiting distribution exists. A displayed prefix of an infinite geometric law must retain its omitted tail qm.

11. Memorylessness and the converse

For nonnegative integers m,n with P(T>m)>0,

P(T>m+n∣T>m)=qm+n/qm=qn.

Equivalently T-m, conditional on surviving past trial m, has the original positive waiting law. The elapsed time is not forgotten; the distribution of the remaining trials is unchanged.

The zero-based variable requires careful wording: P(F≥m+n∣F≥m)=qn. Replacing both weak inequalities by the same strict inequalities changes the offset and may yield a wrong identity.

For the converse, suppose a positive integer-valued proper waiting law has survival am=P(T>m), with a0=1, and am+n=aman. Repeatedly setting n=1 gives am=a1m. Properness forces a1<1. Differences at-1-at give the geometric PMF with p=1-a1. If survival ever becomes zero immediately, the deterministic T=1 case is included.

A waiting law with a time-varying success probability has P(T>m)=∏i=1m(1-pi) and is generally not memoryless. A mixture over a shared hidden p is also generally not geometric: survival conditions reweight the hidden parameter toward smaller probabilities.

12. Capping, truncation and administrative failure codes

These operations are mathematically distinct. A capped trial count C=min(T,m) has ordinary geometric masses for 1≤t<m and terminal mass P(T≥m)=qm-1 at m. That terminal atom includes both success at the last trial and all later success times.

A truncated law, conditional on success by m, has

P(T=t∣T≤m)=qt-1p1-qm,1≤t≤m.

Its normalizer is required. A failure code that reports zero when no success occurs by m has mass qm at zero and mass qt-1p at each reported successful time t≤m. That code is not the capped count.

For the capped count, tail sums give E[C]=(1-qm)/p. For its second moment use C2=∑i=1C(2i-1), so E[C2]=∑i=1m(2i-1)qi-1. These finite sums require no approximation or fabricated infinite tail.

13. Parallel waits, races and ties

For independent positive geometric waits Ti with probabilities pi, their minimum has survival ∏iqim and is geometric with success probability 1-∏iqi. Their maximum has CDF ∏i(1-qim) for integer m≥0 and is generally not geometric.

With two waits, distinguish strict victory from a tie:

P(T1<T2)=∑t≥1p1q1t-1q2t=p1q21-q1q2,
P(T1=T2)=p1p21-q1q2.

Together with the reverse strict victory, these probabilities sum to one. The continuous-race intuition that ties have probability zero is wrong on the discrete time lattice.

For iid waits with failure probability q, inclusion–exclusion in the maximum tail gives

E[maxiTi]=∑j=1m(-1)j+1(mj)11-qj.

The formula follows by expanding 1-(1-qt)m and summing each geometric tail. The number m of competitors is fixed, and 0≤q<1 ensures convergence.

14. Negative-binomial waiting: the forced final success

Let Tr count trials through the r th success, where r is a positive integer and trials are iid with 0<p≤1. For t≥r, the final trial succeeds, and the preceding t-1 positions contain exactly r-1 successes:

P(Tr=t)=(t-1r-1)prqt-r.

The binomial coefficient (tr) would also count sequences whose r th success occurs before the terminal trial, contradicting the stopping definition. The failure count Fr=Tr-r has

P(Fr=f)=(f+r-1r-1)prqf,f≥0.

The waiting increments between successive successes are independent positive geometric waits. To justify independence, specify any finite vector of increment lengths: the required disjoint blocks have probability equal to the product of their geometric masses. Therefore

E[Tr]=r/p,E[Fr]=rq/p,Var(Tr)=Var(Fr)=rq/p2.

The count–wait duality is an event identity:

P(Tr≤n)=P(Sn≥r).

It converts a waiting-time CDF into a binomial upper tail; it does not identify the two random variables. At p=1, the total wait is r; at r=1 it reduces to the positive geometric law.

15. Negative-binomial algebra, modes and generalized shapes

For the failure convention,

GFr(z)=(p1-qz)r,|qz|<1.

Independent failure counts with the same p add their shapes. Unequal probabilities do not generally give a negative-binomial law with a common averaged parameter.

For adjacent failure masses,

P(Fr=f+1)P(Fr=f)=qf+rf+1.

When r>1, the modes are determined by (r-1)q/p: the floor is unique unless that quantity is a positive integer a, in which case a-1 and a tie. For r=1 and p>0, the mode is zero. Add r to convert failure modes into total-wait modes.

The distribution also extends to a positive real shape by replacing the combinatorial coefficient with Γ(f+r)/(Γ(r)f!). To verify this extension, expand A(z)=(1-qz)-r near zero. Its differential equation (1-qz)A'(z)=rqA(z) gives coefficient recursion a0=1 and af+1=q(f+r)af/(f+1). Therefore af=qfr(r+1)…(r+f-1)/f!, which is nonnegative. At z equal to one its sum is p-r, so multiplying by pr normalizes the coefficients. This establishes a genuine law, not merely a symbolic substitution into an integer formula.

The resulting PGF is (p/(1-qz))r; differentiating at one gives first factorial moment rq/p and second factorial moment r(r+1)q2/p2. Restoring the first moment and subtracting the squared mean gives variance rq/p2. A noninteger shape still has no literal interpretation as waiting for a noninteger number of successes. Later continuous-mixture theory can derive it from a gamma-mixed Poisson rate. The present chapter keeps that extension distinct from the iid trial-count construction.

16. Hypergeometric sampling and exact support

Choose a uniform subset of size n from a population of N objects containing K successes. The success count H has

P(H=h)=(Kh)(N-Kn-h)(Nn).

Its positive-mass support is

max(0,n-N+K)≤h≤min(n,K).

The upper limit reflects both the sample size and the success pool. The lower limit prevents requesting more failures than exist. Writing the broader range 0,…,n is acceptable only if impossible masses are assigned zero.

The numerator chooses a success subset and a failure subset; the denominator counts every possible sample. Vandermonde's identity proves normalization by partitioning all samples according to their success counts.

The same formula follows from uniform ordered sampling without replacement: every subset has n! orders, so those factors cancel. Treating each draw as an independent Bernoulli trial with the original success fraction ignores depletion.

17. Finite-population moments, ratios and symmetry

Let p=K/N and N>1. Draw-position indicators each have mean p, and two distinct positions have joint success probability K(K-1)/(N(N-1)). Hence their covariance is -pq/(N-1). Summing every diagonal and ordered off-diagonal contribution gives

E[H]=np,Var(H)=npqN-nN-1.

The correction equals zero for a complete sample. It approaches one when the sampling fraction is small, but is never a license to declare the exact law binomial. The one-object population is deterministic and is handled directly; its variance formula cannot divide by zero.

For feasible adjacent indices,

P(H=h+1)P(H=h)=(K-h)(n-h)(h+1)(N-K-n+h+1).

The ratio decides the mode while retaining tied cases and respecting effective support. The usual mode candidate is ⌊(n+1)(K+1)/(N+2)⌋; if the unfloored value is an interior integer, the adjacent lower value also ties. Verify endpoint cases through the ratio rather than dividing by an impossible zero mass.

Population-complement symmetry turns H into the sample failure count n-H. Sample-complement symmetry turns it into K-H for the unselected subset. A third counting identity exchanges n and K in the hypergeometric count formula. These are law relationships, not statements that different experiments yield the same realized count.

18. Stopping without replacement: negative-hypergeometric waiting

Let Tr be the position of the r th success in a uniform random ordering of a population with K successes among N objects, where 1≤r≤K. A uniformly chosen set of K success positions makes the probability

P(Tr=t)=(t-1r-1)(N-tK-r)(NK),r≤t≤N-K+r.

The last observed position is forced to be successful. Choose r-1 earlier success positions and K-r later success positions. This is finite-population waiting, so geometric memorylessness fails.

There are K+1 gaps of failures before, between and after the success positions. A success-position set is equivalent to a weak composition of N-K failures into those gaps. Symmetry makes every gap have mean (N-K)/(K+1). The r th success follows r leading gaps and r successes, giving

E[Tr]=r(N+1)K+1.

Here is the moment derivation rather than an appeal to a table. Write F=N-K and d=K+1. There are (F+d-1d-1) weak compositions, all equally likely because each corresponds to exactly one success-position subset. For one gap, the generating sum of the falling factorial (g)j is j!zj/(1-z)j+1. The remaining d-1 gaps contribute (1-z)-(d-1). Dividing the coefficient of zF by the total number of compositions gives

E[(G)j]=j!(F)jd(d+1)…(d+j-1).

In particular, E[G]=F/d and E[G(G-1)]=2F(F-1)/(d(d+1)). Add the first moment to obtain the second raw moment, then subtract the squared mean:

Var(G)=F(d-1)(F+d)d2(d+1).

Exchangeability and the constant gap total give 0=dVar(G)+d(d-1)Cov(Gi,Gj) for distinct gaps when d>1. Hence Cov(Gi,Gj)=-F(F+d)/(d2(d+1)). The rth success position is r plus the sum of its r preceding gaps. Including both diagonal variances and ordered cross terms yields

Var(Tr)=r(K-r+1)(N+1)(N-K)(K+1)2(K+2).

These moment identities can be checked directly from the displayed finite PMF. After observing a failure, the remaining population has changed; there is no fresh identical wait. The failure-before-stop convention subtracts r from Tr and leaves its variance unchanged.

19. Poisson counts, factorial moments and units

For λ≥0,

P(X=k)=e-λλkk!,k=0,1,….

The exponential series establishes normalization. At λ=0, all mass is at zero. For a positive parameter, shifting the factorial sum gives

E[(X)j]=λj,E[X]=Var(X)=λ.

The PGF is exp(λ(z-1)). Equal mean and variance are necessary for a Poisson law but do not identify it: a finite two-point law can satisfy the same moments.

The adjacent ratio is λ/(k+1). If λ is not an integer, its floor is the unique mode. If λ=m is a positive integer, both m-1 and m are modes. At zero there is only the deterministic mode zero.

For a homogeneous Poisson process with rate ρ per unit time, the count over exposure t has parameter λ=ρt. The rate carries inverse-time units; the PMF parameter is an expected count. Constant mean rate by itself does not imply independent increments or Poisson counts. A finite interval can contain multiple arrivals. The correct small-interval statements are P(N(h)=1)=ρh+o(h) and P(N(h)≥2)=o(h).

20. Superposition, conditional allocation and independent splitting

Independent Poisson counts with parameters λ1,λ2 have sum parameter λ1+λ2, by PGF multiplication or convolution. Conditional on their sum n,

P(X=k∣X+Y=n)=(nk)(λ1λ1+λ2)k(λ2λ1+λ2)n-k,

provided the total rate is positive and the conditioning event has positive probability.

If a Poisson total of mean λ is independently classified with probabilities a1,…,am, the joint PGF is

exp(λ(∑iaizi-1))=∏iexp(λai(zi-1)).

The factorization proves that category counts are independent Poisson with means λai. Given the total, those same category counts are multinomial and dependent. Conditional and unconditional independence must be stated separately.

A random rate Λ produces a mixed Poisson law. Total variance gives E[X]=E[Λ] and Var(X)=E[Λ]+Var(Λ) when the required moments exist. An excess variance can reveal heterogeneity, but it does not uniquely identify a mixing distribution.

21. Rare-event limits with an explicit error interpretation

For fixed λ and k, a binomial law with p=λ/n has

P(Sn=k)=λkk!(∏j=0k-1(1-j/n))(1-λ/n)n(1-λ/n)-k.

As n tends to infinity with n≥λ, the factors tend respectively to one, e-λ and one. This proves the Poisson point-mass limit. It is not an assertion that every finite binomial tail equals a Poisson tail or that k may grow arbitrarily with n in this argument.

A useful quantitative bound has a short coupling derivation. A Bernoulli variable with probability p and a Poisson variable of mean p have total variation distance p(1-e-p)≤p2: the sole positive difference of Bernoulli mass over Poisson mass is at one. Couple them so that their mismatch probability is that distance, using their common masses first. Independently couple each pair of coordinates. A union bound shows that the two sums disagree with probability at most ∑ipi2.

Thus for independent unequal rare indicators and a Poisson law with λ=∑ipi, every count event has absolute probability error at most min(1,∑ipi2). This is an absolute, not relative, bound. A small bound can still be large relative to an extremely rare tail. Dependence requires a separate argument; the same mean and small marginal probabilities do not automatically justify this certificate.

22. Shared latent parameters and censored observations

Suppose a single hidden probability P is drawn and then n trials are conditionally independent given P. The count law is a mixture of binomial laws:

P(Sn=k)=E[(nk)Pk(1-P)n-k].

It usually differs from Bin(n,E[P]). Total variance gives

Var(Sn)=np¯(1-p¯)+n(n-1)Var(P),p¯=E[P].

The shared parameter contributes positive dependence. By contrast, drawing a fresh independent parameter for every trial can produce independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p¯.

A success-only waiting log samples a truncated law. A log that includes capped failures samples a censored law. If the experiment stops because an outcome-dependent rule is satisfied, the observed count cannot be analyzed by silently treating that horizon as fixed.

For example, a family-size prior and the observation of no boys combine as prior mass times a likelihood 2-n. The likelihood reweights the prior over sizes; the posterior success probability is not obtained by conditioning each individual child independently and retaining the original size distribution.

23. Numerically reliable discrete probabilities

For a moderate binomial parameter, direct factorial products can overflow before the final small probability is formed. Work in log space:

logP(Sn=k)=logΓ(n+1)-logΓ(k+1)-logΓ(n-k+1)+klogp+(n-k)logq.

Handle p=0,1 before logarithms. A log-mass remains meaningful even when its exponential underflows. Adjacent ratios can build a local PMF from a mode without starting from an underflowed endpoint.

For tiny success probabilities, compute qn as exp(nlog(1-p)) with a numerical log-one-plus routine, and compute 1-qn with a numerical exp-minus-one routine. Subtracting two nearly equal rounded numbers loses significant digits. For upper tails, sum the upper-tail masses directly rather than always subtracting a near-one CDF.

The following exact-rational dynamic program computes an independent unequal-trial count. It does not use random simulation as a substitute for a probability law.

from fractions import Fraction

def independent_count(probabilities):
    masses = [Fraction(1)]
    for probability in probabilities:
        p = Fraction(probability)
        if not 0 <= p <= 1:
            raise ValueError("Every probability must be between zero and one.")
        next_masses = [Fraction(0)] * (len(masses) + 1)
        for k, mass in enumerate(masses):
            next_masses[k] += (1 - p) * mass
            next_masses[k + 1] += p * mass
        masses = next_masses
    assert sum(masses) == 1
    return masses

Uniform integer laws and transformed lattices

A variable uniform on the integers one through m assigns each integer mass 1/m. It has mean (m+1)/2. The identity ∑k=1mk2=m(m+1)(2m+1)/6 gives its second raw moment (m+1)(2m+1)/6, and subtraction of the squared mean gives variance (m2-1)/12. These sum identities follow by telescoping successive squares and cubes, respectively, so the formulas also hold at the constant-law boundary m equal to one.

For a uniform variable on integers a through b, let m=b-a+1 and shift the preceding law by a minus one. The mean becomes (a+b)/2, while the variance remains (m2-1)/12. A nonzero affine scale preserves equal atom probabilities but changes the support spacing. For example, Y=2X-3 with X uniform on one through m is uniform on the odd arithmetic progression from minus one through 2m-3, not on every integer between those endpoints. A zero scale instead collapses all mass to one value.

For an event bounded by real thresholds, first solve the inequality for X and then intersect its admissible integer endpoints with the declared support. Conditioning on a retained subset divides its atom probabilities by that subset's probability. A subset containing gaps need not be a consecutive-integer uniform law, even though its retained atoms remain equally weighted.

Uniform lattice under Y = 2X - 3

24. Complete-sentence summary

A distribution name compresses an experiment only when its assumptions are satisfied. A binomial law counts common-probability independent successes on a fixed horizon. A positive geometric law counts trials through a first success; its failure-based version subtracts one. A negative-binomial law stops at the required final success and uses a coefficient counting only preceding success positions. Hypergeometric counts use uniform finite-population sampling without replacement and an effective support constrained by both pools. Finite-population stopping has a negative-hypergeometric law and changed hazards. A Poisson parameter is the expected count over the specified exposure, and its unbounded support differs from a finite binomial support.

PGFs distinguish independent sums from scaled copies, express thinning as composition and recover factorial moments from derivatives. Adjacent ratios identify tied modes without guesswork. Count–wait duality translates events but does not identify random variables. Conditioning can create dependence; Poisson splitting can remove the dependence induced by a fixed total. Truncation, capping and failure codes place different masses at their endpoints. Mixtures over shared parameters change both probabilities and covariance. Approximation statements require an error scale and a declared limiting regime. Every calculation should end with checks of support, normalization, parameter units and the event's strict or non-strict threshold.

Question 1. Heads in a conditional second toss

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MS CE 1405 · Q35 · PDF page 8. Original examination bridge; independently derived answer, not an official key. This previously delivered item is revisited with a deeper named-law interpretation; the audit records its original PDF check.

Four fair coins are tossed. Every coin that showed heads is tossed again. If Y is the number of heads in the second toss, what is P(Y=2)?

1.
1/2
2.
3/4
3.
17/128
4.
27/128
Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 4.

  1. Model each coin by two independent fair tosses, with the second revealed only when the first is heads. A coin contributes one to Y exactly on the outcome heads-heads, which has probability 1/4.
  2. The four contribution indicators are independent, so Y is binomial with parameters 4 and 1/4. Exactly two successes have probability (42)(1/4)2(3/4)2=27/128, option 4.
  3. An independent derivation conditions on the number K of first-round heads. Sum (4k)2-4(k2)2-k for k=2,3,4. The contributions are 3/32,3/32,3/128, whose sum is 27/128.
  4. Treating the second round as four unconditional fair tosses ignores that only first-round heads qualify. Fixing the random number of qualifying coins at its expected value also changes the distribution.

Transfer rule. Replace a multistage selection experiment by independent per-object indicators when eligibility and success can be combined into one event.

1/3

2.

Question 4. Recover a binomial experiment

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A binomial count has mean 6 and variance 4. Recover its parameters and explain why both moments are needed.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For a nondegenerate binomial variable, μ=np and v=np(1-p). Dividing gives 1-p=v/μ=2/3, hence p=1/3 and n=18. Both recovered parameters satisfy their domains. A mean of six alone admits infinitely many trial counts and probabilities, including n=6,p=1. The variance resolves that ambiguity within the binomial family; it does not prove that the unspecified experiment is binomial. Mutual independence, a fixed horizon and a common success probability must still be justified.

Question 5. Reject impossible binomial moments

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Can a binomial variable have mean 3 and variance 2? Can it instead have mean 3 and variance 5/2? Also assess mean 3 and variance 7/3.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first pair gives p=1-2/3=1/3 and n=3/(1/3)=9, so it is feasible. The second gives p=1-5/6=1/6 and n=18, which is also feasible. Now compare mean three and variance 7/3: they give p=2/9 and n=27/2, which is not an integer, so that pair is impossible in the ordinary binomial family. Checking only 0≤v≤μ is necessary but insufficient. The implied trial count must be a nonnegative integer.

Question 6. A parameter from neighboring masses

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(8,p), suppose P(X=3)=2P(X=2)>0. Find p and the modes.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The ratio is P(X=3)P(X=2)=8-23p1-p=2p1-p. Thus p/(1-p)=1, giving p=1/2. Since (n+1)p=9/2 is not an integer, the unique mode is its floor, four. The positivity assumption rules out endpoint cases where division by a zero mass would be invalid. The ratio uses adjacent counts and the fixed value of n; comparing masses separated by several indices requires a product of ratios.

Question 7. Tied binomial modes

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Find all modes of X∼Bin(9,2/5) and justify the tie rather than rounding its mean.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The ratio from k to k+1 equals (9-k)2/[3(k+1)]. It exceeds one for k<3, equals one at k=3, and is below one afterward. Therefore counts three and four are both modes. Equivalently, (n+1)p=4 is an integer, producing modes three and four. The mean is 18/5, whose nearest integer happens to be four but would lose the equally probable count three. The mode is a maximizer of probability mass, not an estimate obtained by rounding expectation.

Question 8. A fair-count strict threshold

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Eight fair independent coins are tossed. Find the probability of fewer than four heads without adding four separate binomial terms.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Reflection exchanges heads and tails, so P(X<4)=P(X>4). The central mass is P(X=4)=(84)/28=70/256. The remaining probability splits equally, giving P(X<4)=(1-70/256)/2=93/256. Fewer than four excludes the central count; at most four would add 70/256. The symmetry argument requires a fair coin. It would not justify equal tails for a biased success probability, even if the threshold were located near the mean.

Question 9. Parity from a PGF

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(5,1/3), find P(X is even) and explain the role of evaluation at minus one.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Write e=P(X even) and o=P(X odd). Then e+o=G(1)=1 and e-o=G(-1)=(2/3-1/3)5=1/243. Solving gives e=(1+1/243)/2=122/243. The alternating signs select parity because (-1)k is positive at even indices and negative at odd indices. This method sums all admissible even masses at once. It is valid for a probability generating function at minus one; it is not a claim that a negative number is a probability.

Question 10. Condition on a fixed total

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Six independent Bernoulli trials have common 0<p<1. Given exactly two successes in all six, find the probability of exactly one success among the first three.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Every two-success set has the same unconditional weight p2(1-p)4, so conditioning makes the (62)=15 sets uniform. To obtain one success in each half, choose one position from each three-position block, giving nine sets. The probability is 9/15=3/5. The conditional first-half count is hypergeometric, not an independent binomial with probability 1/3. The value of p cancels because all conditioned configurations share it; unequal trial probabilities would destroy the uniform-set conclusion.

Question 12. Classify successes into competing labels

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

In five independent trials, an A outcome has probability 1/4, a B outcome probability 1/2, and otherwise neither occurs. Find the covariance of their counts and P(A=1,B=2).

Question 13. Third factorial moment and ordinary third moment

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(7,2/5), derive E[X3] without expanding seven indicators cubically.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Question 14. A zero-truncated binomial law

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(4,1/2), compute E[X∣X>0] and Var(X∣X>0).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The conditioning probability is 15/16. Since the excluded value is zero, the first and second raw numerator moments remain E[X]=2 and E[X2]=Var(X)+E[X]2=5. Thus the conditional moments are 32/15 and 16/3. Subtract their squared mean to obtain 16/3-1024/225=176/225. Dividing the unconditional variance by 15/16 is wrong because conditional variance must use the conditional center. The positive-conditioned law has support one through four and is not an ordinary binomial law.

Question 15. Unequal independent trial probabilities

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Three independent trials have success probabilities 1/2,1/3,1/4. Find the full success-count law and compare its variance with a same-mean binomial law.

The same-mean binomial would have p=13/36 and variance 3p(1-p)=299/432, exceeding 285/432 by 7/216. Equal mean does not identify equal laws. The difference measures probability heterogeneity, not dependence.

Question 16. Pairwise independence is insufficient

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Let U,V be independent fair bits, and let W=UxorV. Is U+V+W binomial? Find its law.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The four equally likely pairs (U,V) produce triples 000,011,101,110. Every two coordinates are independent fair bits, but all three are not mutually independent: their parity is always even. The sum is zero with probability 1/4 and two with probability 3/4. Its mean is 3/2 and variance 3/4, the same as Bin(3,1/2), yet its support excludes one and three. This counterexample simultaneously disproves inferring a binomial law from pairwise independence or from matching its first two moments.

A fair binomial would have variance 3/2 and all-zero mass 1/64. Conditional independence does not imply unconditional independence when trials share P. The excess variance quantifies the shared-parameter contribution; it is not numerical error.

Question 28. Minimum and maximum waits

The minimum survives m trials only when both clocks do, so its survival is (q1q2)m=(1/3)m. It is positive geometric with success probability 2/3, giving mean 3/2. Pointwise, the minimum plus the maximum equals the sum of the two waits. Their individual means are three and two, hence the maximum has mean 5-3/2=7/2. The maximum is not geometric: its survival is q1m+q2m-(q1q2)m. Independence is needed for the product survival, not for the pointwise sum identity.

Question 29. Waiting with changing hazards

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

On trial i, an independent attempt succeeds with probability pi=1/(i+1). Find P(T>m) and decide whether the first-success wait has finite mean.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Independence gives P(T>m)=∏i=1m(1-pi)=∏i=1mi/(i+1)=1/(m+1). This survival tends to zero, so success eventually occurs almost surely. However, the positive-integer tail-sum mean is ∑m=0∞1/(m+1), which diverges. Almost-sure finite completion therefore does not imply finite expected duration. The hazards change with elapsed trials, so neither a constant-p geometric law nor its memoryless formula applies.

Question 30. A mixture destroys memorylessness

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Choose p equally from 1/4,3/4 once, and then wait for a success in conditionally independent trials. Compare P(T>2∣T>1) with P(T>1).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The initial one-trial survival is the average failure probability, 1/2. Two-trial survival averages squared failure probabilities: 12[(3/4)2+(1/4)2]=5/16. Therefore conditional residual one-trial survival is (5/16)/(1/2)=5/8, not 1/2. Observing a failure increases posterior weight on the low-success regime. Conditional geometric behavior given p does not establish an unconditional geometric law. The same hidden parameter persists through the experiment; choosing a fresh independent p each trial would have a different result.

Question 31. Recover a geometric law from memorylessness

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A positive-integer variable T satisfies P(T>m+n)=P(T>m)P(T>n) for all nonnegative integers. If P(T>1)=3/5, derive its full law.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Let am=P(T>m); positive support gives a0=1. The identity with n equal to one yields am+1=am(3/5), so induction gives am=(3/5)m. Taking successive survival differences produces P(T=k)=(3/5)k-1(2/5) for positive k. Thus T is geometric with success probability 2/5. Its mean is 5/2. The support and the survival identity establish the law; knowing a single tail probability alone would not suffice.

Trial five must succeed, and the first four trials must contain exactly one success. There are (41)=4 valid arrangements, each with probability p2q3. Thus the required probability is 4(1/4)2(3/4)3=27/256. Using (52) includes arrangements whose second success occurred before trial five and whose final trial failed. A fixed-horizon count of two successes and a stopped wait through two successes describe different events, although they are related by count–wait duality.

Question 35. An independent sum with a common parameter

Each wait has PGF (pz/(1-qz))r under the total-trial convention. Independence multiplies the two PGFs, giving (pz/(1-qz))5. This is the total-trial negative-binomial wait through five successes. Its mean is 5/p and variance 5q/p2. The separate experiment interpretation avoids double-counting a single timeline. Question 37. Tied negative-binomial modes

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For the failure count before three successes with p=1/3, find all modes.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The ratio of masses at f plus one and f is q(f+r)/(f+1)=2(f+3)/[3(f+1)]. It equals one when f equals three, exceeds one at smaller indices and is below one at larger indices. Therefore failure counts three and four are tied modes. Total-trial modes are obtained by adding r, giving six and seven. The failure-count mode formula involves (r-1)q/p; its integral value creates a tie one count earlier. Applying a binomial mode rule to this unbounded stopped count is invalid.

Question 38. A conditional residual wait after a partial count

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A trial sequence has common success probability 1/3. Given that the first five trials contain exactly one success, how much longer on average is needed to reach three successes in total?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The conditioning depends only on the first five trials. Independence leaves the future sequence unchanged, and two additional successes are required. Its extra wait is a total-trial negative-binomial variable with r equal to two and mean 2/(1/3)=6. Thus the conditional total finishing-trial expectation is eleven. It is not nine, the unconditional mean wait for three successes. Elapsed trials and remaining successes are separate state variables. If past information also updated a shared unknown success parameter, the future law would need posterior mixing.

Question 39. The second moment of a stopped wait

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For the total wait T through four successes with p=2/3, find E[T2] and the covariance of T with its failure count F.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The mean is r/p=6, and variance is rq/p2=4(1/3)/(4/9)=3. Consequently E[T2]=3+36=39. Since F=T-4, covariance is Cov(T,F)=Cov(T,T-4)=Var(T)=3. The same random variable shifted by a constant is perfectly positively correlated when variance is nonzero. T and F are not independent merely because one counts all trials and the other only failures. Their deterministic relation should be used before attempting a joint probability calculation.

Question 40. A binomial horizon mistaken for a stopping horizon

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

An observer reports exactly three successes in ten trials with probability p. Another observer reports the third success occurring at trial ten. Compare their event probabilities.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The fixed-horizon event has probability (103)p3q7. The stopped event forces the tenth trial to be a success and chooses the other two among the first nine, giving (92)p3q7. Their ratio is (92)/(103)=3/10, independent of p when both probabilities are positive. Given exactly three successes among ten, each of the three success positions is uniformly distributed over the ten positions, so the final trial is successful with probability 3/10. The distinction is a support and combinatorial constraint, not a change in trial probability.

Question 41. Success before a failure budget is exhausted

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Successes win exactly when the third success occurs with zero or one preceding failures. The two probabilities are p3 and (31)p3q, totaling p3(1+3q)=16/27. Equivalently, among the first four trials at least three are successes, whose binomial probability is 4p3q+p4=16/27. Question 42. An exponential tilt of a geometric law

Let F have failure-based geometric parameter p. Reweight its masses by af with a≥0. When does normalization exist, and what is the resulting law?

The unnormalized weights are p(aq)f. Their sum is p/(1-aq) exactly when aq<1. Dividing gives masses (1-aq)(aq)f, a failure-based geometric law with new success parameter 1-aq. At a=0, all mass is at zero; when aq≥1 the sum diverges and no normalized probability law exists. The tilt changes the distribution of the entire count. This algebra explains geometric posterior updates under an exponentially decreasing likelihood, without treating a likelihood itself as a normalized prior.

Question 56. A Poisson parity identity

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Question 57. A Poisson fourth moment

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

The derivative order and the ordinary exponent cannot be interchanged: the fourth PGF derivative at one gives only the fourth falling-factorial moment. At parameter zero every term vanishes, consistent with a constant zero variable. This method avoids an infinite direct sum while retaining repeated-index corrections.

An observed Poisson count is sampled with probability proportional to its count, so its new PMF is kP(X=k)/E[X]. Identify the resulting distribution for positive parameter.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The size-biased mass at positive k is ke-λλk/(k!λ)=e-λλk-1/(k-1)!. Hence the observed variable equals one plus a Poisson variable of the same parameter. Its mean is 1+λ and variance lambda. The zero mass disappears because a zero-count object cannot be selected by this rule. This is different from conditioning on positivity, which renormalizes each positive mass uniformly rather than multiplying it by its count.

Question 65. A finite sum is not a scaled copy

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For independent Poisson variables X1 and X2 of parameter two, compare X1+X2 with 2X1.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Independence gives X1+X2∼Pois(4), with mean and variance four and full nonnegative-integer support. The scaled copy has mean four, variance 4Var(X1)=8, and support restricted to even integers. Its PGF is GX1(z2), while the independent sum uses GX1(z)2. Similar notation for addition and multiplication can hide distinct dependence structures. The means agreeing is not evidence of equal distributions or equal variances.

Question 66. A rare-event approximation with a checked error

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(200,1/200), write the exact probability of at most one success, the Poisson approximation and a rigorous absolute error bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The exact probability is (199/200)200+(199/200)199. With parameter np=1, the Poisson approximation is 2e-1. Coupling each Bernoulli coordinate with an independent Poisson coordinate gives an event-probability error bounded by ∑pi2=200/2002=1/200. The event probability, rather than each mass separately, obeys this bound. It is an absolute bound and does not imply a small relative error for a rare event. A printed rule of thumb about n and p alone is weaker than this quantified statement.

Question 67. A bound for heterogeneous rare trials

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Independent trials have probabilities 0.01,0.02,0.03. Approximate their no-success probability and give a bound without treating them as identically distributed.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The exact probability is 0.99·0.98·0.97=0.941094. The Poisson parameter is the probability sum, 0.06, so the approximation is e-0.06, about 0.9417645. The coupling bound is 0.012+0.022+0.032=0.0014, which exceeds the actual absolute discrepancy of about 0.0006705. No common probability was assumed. Using Bin(3,0.02) as if it were exact would introduce a different approximation before the Poisson step.

Question 68. Prove the one-coordinate coupling distance

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Compute the total-variation distance between a Bernoulli variable of parameter p and a Poisson variable of parameter p, for 0≤p≤1.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

At zero, the Poisson mass e-p is at least 1-p by the exponential inequality. At one, Bernoulli has excess mass p-pe-p. At all larger indices, only Poisson has positive mass. Total variation is the sum of the positive Bernoulli excesses, so it equals p(1-e-p)≤p2. Matching the shared masses at each index constructs a coupling with this discrepancy probability. The bound is not an equality in general; the exact distance is the first expression. It compares laws, not numerical simulations.

Question 69. A fixed-k limit is not uniform over moving k

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For Xn∼Bin(n,λ/n), explain why pointwise convergence of P(Xn=k) for each fixed k does not by itself certify an approximation at k=n.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The standard limit holds k fixed while n grows; its finite product and factorial approximations rely on that regime. A moving count k equal to n is not covered by those steps. The binomial mass there is (λ/n)n, while the Poisson mass is e-λλn/n!, with a ratio involving n!/nn that changes drastically. Both masses can be tiny, so absolute and relative errors tell different stories. A uniform event bound needs a separate coupling or total-variation argument, not a relabeled pointwise proof.

Question 70. Shared dependence can break rare-event reasoning

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Let each of n indicators equal the same Bernoulli variable B of parameter 1/n. Does their sum approach a Poisson law of parameter one?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The sum is nB, so it is zero with probability 1-1/n and n with probability 1/n. Every individual probability is small and the mean sum is one, yet the all-zero probability tends to one instead of e-1. The indicators are perfectly dependent. The independent-coordinate coupling bound cannot be applied. Even the mean fails to pass to the limiting constant-zero law because the rare n-sized values retain mean one. Small marginals and a matched intensity do not establish Poisson approximation.

Question 71. A small-interval process statement

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A homogeneous Poisson process has rate ρ. Is its count in an interval of positive length h exactly Bernoulli? State the correct small-h relations.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The interval count is Poisson with parameter ρh and has positive probability of two or more events whenever ρh>0. Therefore it is not exactly Bernoulli. Its one-event probability is ρhe-ρh=ρh+O(h2), and its multiple-event probability is 1-e-ρh(1+ρh)=O(h2). Together with independent disjoint increments, these asymptotic relations support the process limit. Describing an arbitrarily short finite interval as exactly binary silently drops nonzero mass.

Question 72. A discrete uniform transform

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Let X be uniform on integers one through m, and set Y=2X-3. Find support, mean and variance, and decide whether Y is uniform on every integer between its endpoints.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The image support is -1,1,3,…,2m-3, with mass 1/m at each image because the transform is injective. The mean is 2(m+1)/2-3=m-2, and variance is 4(m2-1)/12=(m2-1)/3. Y is uniform on this arithmetic progression, not on all intervening integers: even indices have zero probability. An affine transform preserves equal atom weights but can change lattice spacing. At m equal to one, the variable is constant and variance is zero.

Question 73. An integer threshold under a lattice transform

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X uniform on one through eight and Y=3X+1, find P(8<Y≤20) and E[Y∣8<Y≤20].

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The inequalities become 7/3<X≤19/3, so the admissible integers are three through six. Four of the eight equally likely values qualify, giving probability one half. Their transformed values are ten, thirteen, sixteen and nineteen, whose conditional mean is 58/4=29/2. The conditional X mean is 9/2, and applying the affine map gives the same result. Rounding both original thresholds in the same direction would include or exclude an incorrect boundary atom.

Question 74. Normalization at a binomial endpoint

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

What are the laws of a binomial count with n=0, and of a count with n=5,p=1? Why should a software implementation avoid evaluating a general log-mass formula first?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The empty count at n equal to zero is deterministically zero, regardless of p. With five certain successes, the count is deterministically five. The general log expression contains logarithms of p and 1-p and products such as zero times the logarithm of zero, which floating-point arithmetic may treat as undefined. Handle deterministic endpoint laws before logarithms or factorial ratios. This is a boundary interpretation of a valid experiment, not a numerical patch that changes its probability.

Question 75. Compute a stable tiny tail

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(n,p) with very small p, explain how to compute P(X≥1) without cancellation, and distinguish numerical error from modeling error.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The exact probability is 1-(1-p)n. Compute it as -expm1(nlog1p(-p)), using routines designed for tiny arguments. Direct subtraction from one can lose significant digits when the no-success probability rounds near one. This stable formula still describes an independent common-p binomial model. Replacing it by 1-e-np introduces Poisson modeling approximation in addition to numerical evaluation. Good numerical routines do not validate the experimental assumptions or make an approximation exact.

Question 76. Infer a law from a PGF coefficient pattern

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A count has PGF G(z)=(2+z)5/35. Identify its law and obtain P(X≤1) and E[X(X-1)].

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Writing the factor as 2/3+z/3 identifies Bin(5,1/3). The zero mass is 32/243, and the one mass is 5(1/3)(2/3)4=80/243, so the requested lower-tail probability is 112/243. The second derivative at one is 5·4/9=20/9, the second falling-factorial moment. It is not the variance; variance is 5(1/3)(2/3)=10/9. A PGF gives both coefficients and derivatives, but their meanings must remain distinct.

Question 77. A random-sum model

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A Poisson number N of parameter two determines how many independent fair Bernoulli marks are summed. Find the resulting count law and distinguish this from NB for a single common mark.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Independent fresh marks give PGF GN((1+z)/2)=exp(z-1), so the result is Poisson with parameter one. A single common fair mark B instead yields a mixture: zero if B is zero and the entire Poisson count if B is one. Its zero probability is (1+e-2)/2, not e-1, and its variance is two rather than one. Random-sum composition requires independent summands and independence of the summands from N; repeating the same mark creates dependence.

Question 78. Conditional law under a zero observation

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A failure-based geometric family-size prior has parameter one half. Each child independently passes an observation test with probability one half. Given zero passing children, derive the posterior family-size law.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The prior mass at n is 2-n-1 and the likelihood of zero passes is 2-n. Their product is (1/2)4-n. The sum over all nonnegative n is 2/3, so the posterior mass is (3/4)(1/4)n, a failure-based geometric law of parameter 3/4. Its positive-size probability is 1/4 and mean 1/3. The zero-size case satisfies the observation automatically and must be retained. Updating individual outcomes without reweighting family sizes misses the selection effect.

Question 79. Why factorial moments do not justify an arbitrary law

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

An investigator knows E[X]=2 for an integer count but assumes E[X(X-1)]=4 because a Poisson variable has that value. Diagnose the inference and give a counterexample.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A Poisson variable of mean two does have second falling-factorial moment four. However, the constant count X equal to two has the same mean and falling-factorial moment two, not four. Its variance is zero rather than two. The identity E[X2]=E[X(X-1)]+E[X] holds for any variable with finite second moment; substituting a Poisson-specific factorial moment requires establishing the Poisson law first. A mean is an expectation constraint, not a generating-function or full-distribution specification.

Question 80. Choose the family before calculating

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Classify three experiments: successes in eight independent attempts with common p; attempts through the third success; and marks among eight objects drawn without replacement from a finite population.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first is a fixed-horizon binomial count with support zero through eight. The second is a total-trial negative-binomial wait with support three onward when 0<p<1; its last attempt must succeed. The third is hypergeometric with support bounded by both marked and unmarked pools. The number eight names different quantities in the first and third experiments, and there is no deterministic eight-attempt horizon in the second. Correct classification precedes selecting a coefficient, moment formula or tail expression.

Question 81. Conditioning on an impossible event

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(4,0), can one calculate P(X=1∣X>0) by continuity from positive p? Is that an ordinary conditional probability in the stated experiment?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

At p equal to zero, X is identically zero and P(X>0)=0. The usual finite-event conditional ratio is therefore undefined. For positive p, the conditional probability is 4p(1-p)3/[1-(1-p)4], whose limit is one as p approaches zero. That limiting conditional law is a different construction and must be labeled as such. An algebraic limit does not assign a uniquely determined event conditional within a model where the conditioning event has zero probability.

Question 82. A Poisson count conditioned by a parity observation

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For positive λ, derive E[X∣X even] when X is Poisson.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Use E[X(-1)X]=(-1)G′(-1)=-λe-2λ. Since the even indicator equals (1+(-1)X)/2, the even-conditioned first-moment numerator is λ(1-e-2λ)/2. Divide by the even probability (1+e-2λ)/2 to obtain λ(1-e-2λ)/(1+e-2λ). The support contains only even integers, so the conditional law is not Poisson even though its calculation uses the original PGF. Differentiating at minus one requires the extra z factor for E[XzX].

Question 83. A binomial sample conditioned on parity

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For X∼Bin(3,1/2), find its law and variance conditional on an even count.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Only zero and two are admissible. Their original masses are 1/8 and 3/8, totaling one half. The conditional masses are therefore 1/4 and 3/4, with mean 3/2, second moment three and variance 3/4. These moments match the original fair binomial, yet the conditional support is different. This reinforces that even matching both mean and variance does not identify a named family. Conditioning must be applied to each retained atom before computing centered moments.

Question 84. A direct hypergeometric second factorial moment

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

For a uniform n-subset of N objects with K marks, derive E[X(X-1)] and use it to recover variance.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For each ordered pair of distinct sample positions, both are marked with probability K(K-1)/[N(N-1)] when N>1. There are n(n-1) ordered pairs, so the falling-factorial moment is n(n-1)K(K-1)/[N(N-1)]. Add the mean nK/N to get the second raw moment and subtract the squared mean. Simplification yields n(K/N)(1-K/N)(N-n)/(N-1). Ordered pairs explain the absence of a factor one half; unordered pairs instead correspond to (X2).

Question 85. A posterior rate mixture after no events

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A hidden Poisson parameter is one or three with equal prior weights. Given a zero count in one exposure, find the probability the parameter was one and the next equal-exposure expected count.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The zero likelihoods are e-1 and e-3. Bayes normalization gives posterior low-rate weight e-1/(e-1+e-3)=e2/(e2+1). If the next count is conditionally independent given the same hidden parameter, its predictive mean is (e2+3)/(e2+1). This is below the prior mean two because a quiet exposure favors the low-rate regime. Independent increments conditional on an unknown shared rate do not imply unconditional independent observations. Resetting the hidden parameter between exposures would change the predictive update.

Question 86. Repeated until a sampled batch is acceptable

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

Independent batches each contain four fair trials. Continue sampling batches until a batch has at least two successes. Find the expected number of batches and expected total number of trials.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

One batch is acceptable with probability 1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)=1-1/16-4/16=11/16. Independent batches create a positive geometric batch wait with mean 16/11. Each batch always contains four trials, so total trials equal four times the batch count and have mean 64/11. Stopping within a batch at the second success would be a different experiment. Question 87. Stop at the first success among a finite set

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A random permutation of N items contains exactly one mark. Compare its first-mark position law with an independent geometric wait of success probability 1/N.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The unique marked position is uniform on one through N. Its mean is (N+1)/2 and variance (N2-1)/12. An independent replacement wait with probability 1/N instead has mean N, variance N(N-1) and unbounded support. Both experiments have initial success probability 1/N, but after a failed finite-population draw the success hazard rises to 1/(N-i+1). One initial probability does not determine a waiting-time law; how the population or trial process changes afterward matters.
