Question 88. Assess an approximation at impossible finite counts

Original or reconstructed problem · mathematical and conceptual reasoning

Original formula and conceptual examination-style problem

A binomial count has n trials, and a Poisson approximation uses parameter np. What should be reported for a requested probability above n?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The exact binomial probability of a count above n is zero by support. The Poisson approximation assigns a positive tail there when np is positive, because its support is unbounded. If the task asks for the exact answer, report zero before computing any approximation. If it asks to study approximation quality, the Poisson tail is an explicit mismatch and contributes to total variation. An approximation does not alter the support of the original experiment. Absolute smallness may make the tail tolerable for some uses, but it cannot justify describing it as exact.

26. Final reasoning rules and examination traps

Model-selection and examination review sheet

Experimental contracts

Rule 1

Define the random variable before naming its law. State whether it counts successes, failures, trials, marked sample objects or arrivals over an exposure.

Rule 2

A binomial experiment has a fixed integer horizon, mutually independent trials and a common success probability. A familiar-looking coefficient does not establish these assumptions.

Rule 3

Pairwise independence does not imply a binomial law. Three pairwise independent fair bits can have only even total counts.

Rule 4

Matching the first two moments of a named law does not identify that law. Verify its support and probability structure as well.

Rule 5

A random horizon cannot ordinarily be replaced by its expected value. Doing so can preserve a mean while changing the support and variance.

Rule 6

Distinguish unconditional independence from independence conditional on a shared parameter. Mixing over that parameter can create dependence.

Rule 7

Sampling without replacement changes the success hazard after a draw. Use the remaining population, rather than repeating the initial probability.

Rule 8

Separate a success probability from an event rate. A probability is dimensionless; a rate needs a time or exposure unit.

Bernoulli and binomial counts

Rule 9

A Bernoulli variable has support zero and one, mean p and variance p(1-p). Every positive integer power equals the variable itself.

Rule 10

Bernoulli variance is at most one quarter. A variance below this maximum can correspond to two reflected success probabilities.

Rule 11

If 0≤X≤1 and E[X]=E[X2], nonnegativity of X(1-X) forces X to be Bernoulli almost surely. The interval assumption is essential.

Rule 12

The binomial mass is (nk)pk(1-p)n-k on integers zero through n. The coefficient counts distinct success-position sets.

Rule 13

A binomial variable has mean np and variance np(1-p). Zero trials, zero success probability and certain success are legitimate constant-law boundaries.

Rule 14

For positive mean and nondegenerate variance, moment recovery gives p=1-v/μ and n=μ/p. The recovered n must be an integer.

Rule 15

A binomial adjacent-mass ratio is (n-k)p/[(k+1)(1-p)]. Locate its crossing of one to identify modes and ties.

Rule 16

For 0<p<1, a noninteger (n+1)p gives the single mode ⌊(n+1)p⌋. If it is an integer, that integer and its predecessor tie.

Rule 17

The probability of an even binomial count is [1+(1-2p)n]/2. Its PGF at minus one gives even probability minus odd probability.

Rule 18

For a fair even-sized count, the probability strictly below the midpoint is half the probability left after removing the central atom.

Rule 19

Complementing a binomial count changes its success probability to 1-p. A biased law is not generally symmetric around its mean.

Rule 20

Given k total common-probability successes among n trials, their positions form a uniform k-subset. Counts in a sub-block are hypergeometric.

Rule 21

Independent qualification with probability p followed by independent passing with probability a produces per-object success probability pa. Combine the stages before identifying the final count.

Rule 22

Counts of competing labels at a fixed horizon are usually negatively correlated. Their binomial marginals do not imply independent counts.

Rule 23

Independent unequal-probability trials produce a Poisson-binomial count with PGF ∏i(1-pi+piz). The ordinary binomial formula is generally inapplicable.

Rule 24

The heterogeneous-count variance is ∑ipi(1-pi). For a fixed average success probability, it is at most the same-mean binomial variance.

Rule 25

A shared random probability produces variance np¯(1-p¯)+n(n-1)Var(P). Drawing a fresh independent probability each trial is a different model.

Rule 26

Derivatives of a count PGF at one give falling-factorial moments. Convert those moments into ordinary powers before calculating variance or higher raw moments.

First-success waiting

Rule 27

A positive geometric variable counts trials through the first success and has mass p(1-p)t-1 at positive t.

Rule 28

A failure-based geometric variable subtracts one from the positive wait. Its support starts at zero, its mean is (1-p)/p, and its variance remains (1-p)/p2.

Rule 29

Positive geometric survival is P(T>m)=(1-p)m for nonnegative integer m. The distinction between greater-than and greater-than-or-equal changes the exponent.

Rule 30

Convert real thresholds into admissible integer endpoints before applying a discrete survival formula. Fractional exponents do not directly count integer waiting outcomes.

Rule 31

Positive geometric memorylessness gives P(T>m+n∣T>m)=P(T>n). The conditioning event must have positive probability.

Rule 32

Conditional residual waiting has mean 1/p, but the conditional total wait after m failures has mean m+1/p.

Rule 33

The integer survival multiplicative identity, together with positive support, characterizes a geometric law. A single mean or one tail value does not.

Rule 34

For changing independent hazards, survival is a product of failure probabilities. Almost-sure success does not necessarily imply finite expected waiting.

Rule 35

A shared hidden success probability usually destroys unconditional memorylessness. Past failures reweight its posterior distribution.

Rule 36

Capping at c moves every wait at or beyond c onto the endpoint. Its endpoint mass is P(T≥c), not merely P(T=c).

Rule 37

Truncating to successes by c discards other attempts and renormalizes all retained masses by P(T≤c). It differs from capping.

Rule 38

Coding unresolved attempts as zero creates a finite observed law. Its zero label is not automatically a geometric failure count.

Rule 39

For a positive integer variable, the tail-sum mean is ∑m≥0P(T>m). This identity also diagnoses infinite expectations.

Rule 40

Independent discrete waiting clocks can tie. Their minimum has product survival, while their maximum has union survival.

Rule 41

For independent positive geometric clocks, the tie probability is p1p2/[1-(1-p1)(1-p2)]. A continuous-race argument would lose this atom.

Rule 42

Pointwise, the minimum plus the maximum equals the sum of two waits. This expectation identity does not require independence, although the product-survival calculation does.

Multiple successes and finite-population waits

Rule 43

A total-trial negative-binomial wait through r successes has support r onward and mass (t-1r-1)pr(1-p)t-r.

Rule 44

The final trial in a stopped success wait is forced to succeed. Replacing its coefficient with (tr) includes invalid arrangements.

Rule 45

The failure-based negative-binomial variable is the total wait minus r. Its mean is r(1-p)/p and its variance is r(1-p)/p2.

Rule 46

The total-trial negative-binomial mean is r/p. It can be derived by adding independent inter-success geometric increments.

Rule 47

Count–wait duality states P(Tr≤n)=P(Bin(n,p)≥r). It identifies events in a shared sequence, not the two random variables.

Rule 48

Independent negative-binomial counts with the same success probability add their success targets. Different probabilities generally prevent closure in the same family.

Rule 49

Failure-count adjacent ratios equal (1-p)(f+r)/(f+1). Check the crossing of one and valid support before assigning modes.

Rule 50

A noninteger shape extension defines a valid analytic count law for appropriate parameters, but it is not literally the number of trials through a fractional success target.

Rule 51

A hypergeometric count uses a uniform sample without replacement. Its PMF is (Kk)(N-Kn-k)/(Nn).

Rule 52

Hypergeometric effective support is max(0,n-N+K) through min(n,K). Check both marked and unmarked pool constraints.

Rule 53

Hypergeometric mean is nK/N, but its variance differs from replacement sampling by the finite-population factor (N-n)/(N-1) for N>1.

Rule 54

If the whole population is drawn, the marked count is constant. At N=1, use that direct law rather than evaluating an undefined variance ratio.

Rule 55

The complement of a uniform sample is uniform. The number of marks left behind has the corresponding complementary-sample hypergeometric law.

Rule 56

Hypergeometric adjacent ratios use both depleted pools. A mode formula must be checked for ties and clipped to the effective support.

Rule 57

A finite-population rth-mark position has bounded support r through N-K+r. It is negative hypergeometric, not a constant-hazard negative-binomial wait.

Rule 58

The finite rth-mark PMF counts r minus one marks before its endpoint and K minus r afterward. Its denominator counts all K-position subsets.

Rule 59

Uniform mark positions correspond bijectively to uniform weak compositions of the unmarked gaps. Gap symmetry yields the mean wait r(N+1)/(K+1).

Rule 60

Gap variables are exchangeable but dependent because their sum is fixed. Include their negative covariance when calculating a partial-gap sum variance.

Rule 61

A finite-population wait–count event uses a hypergeometric count at the fixed horizon. Changing it to binomial would assume replacement.

Poisson counts, conditioning and approximation

Rule 62

A Poisson count has mass e-λλk/k! at nonnegative integer k. Its mean and variance both equal lambda.

Rule 63

Equal mean and variance do not characterize a Poisson law. A two-point non-Poisson law can share those moments.

Rule 64

A homogeneous rate over exposure t produces parameter λ=ρt. Convert units before multiplying the rate and duration.

Rule 65

A positive finite interval in a Poisson process is not exactly Bernoulli. Multiple events have nonzero probability, even though their small-interval probability is of smaller order.

Rule 66

Poisson adjacent ratios are λ/(k+1). A positive integer lambda gives two modes, lambda minus one and lambda; a noninteger lambda gives its floor.

Rule 67

Poisson falling-factorial moments are powers of lambda. Its ordinary third and fourth moments need the lower-order polynomial corrections.

Rule 68

Independent Poisson counts add their parameters. A scaled copy instead changes lattice spacing and multiplies variance by the square of its scale.

Rule 69

Given the sum of independent Poisson counts, their allocation is binomial or multinomial with probabilities proportional to their parameters.

Rule 70

Independent labeling of a Poisson total creates independent Poisson category counts. Given a fixed total, those category counts are dependent.

Rule 71

A random-intensity mixture has variance equal to its mean plus the variance of its intensity. A shared rate can also make different observations dependent.

Rule 72

Conditioning a Poisson law on positivity requires renormalizing its positive atoms. It differs from size bias, which multiplies masses by their counts.

Rule 73

A size-biased positive-parameter Poisson variable equals one plus a Poisson variable. Verify the sampling mechanism before using this identity.

Rule 74

Rare independent Bernoulli counts can be approximated by a Poisson law with parameter ∑ipi. A coupling gives event-probability error at most ∑ipi2.

Rule 75

An absolute error bound does not imply a relative accuracy guarantee for a tiny event. State which scale the approximation controls.

Rule 76

Fixed-k pointwise limits do not by themselves justify moving-index or uniform approximations. Such claims need a separate argument.

Rule 77

Small individual probabilities and a matched mean are insufficient when rare-event indicators are dependent. A shared indicator gives a direct counterexample.

Rule 78

A finite binomial count cannot exceed its horizon, even when an unbounded Poisson approximation assigns mass there. Exact support takes precedence in exact questions.

Calculation and final checks

Rule 79

Use exact rational arithmetic for small finite laws, log-mass formulas for large factorials, and stable log-one-plus and exp-minus-one routines for tiny tails. Handle endpoint laws first.

Rule 80

Finish every answer by checking support, total probability, parameter domains, units, conditioning direction and strict threshold meaning. A plausible number is not a substitute for a valid experiment.

Rule 81

A variable uniform on consecutive integers a through b has mean (a+b)/2 and variance ((b-a+1)2-1)/12. Count the endpoints when determining the support size.

Rule 82

A nonzero affine map of uniform integer atoms preserves equal probabilities but can change lattice spacing. Missing intermediate integers have probability zero.

Rule 83

A conditioning event of zero probability does not define an ordinary event-ratio conditional law. A limit from nearby models is a separate construction.

Rule 84

A displayed finite prefix of an infinite count law must retain an explicit omitted-tail probability. Renormalizing that prefix changes the law to a truncated one.

27. Editable distribution laboratory

Counts n are bounded by twelve, population N by thirty, success target r by six and Poisson parameter by eight. The display limit is one through twelve: geometric waits show that many positive trial positions; negative-binomial waits show failure counts zero through that limit, shifted by r; Poisson counts show zero through the limit. Irrelevant parameters do not change the selected experiment. Displayed prefixes retain their omitted probability and use a fixed vertical scale from zero through one. Invalid input preserves the preceding valid result. The calculator uses floating-point probabilities; it does not infer whether an observed experiment satisfies the selected model.
